item.title: How Do Tiny Plants Help Keep Microplastics Out of the Ocean?
item.description: A clever new invention mimics the way ultrahydrophobic plants in wetlands trap microplastic particles, and it is already pulling more than 98% of them out of wastewater flowing toward the Atlantic Ocean.

item.title: Could Coconut Oil Power the Next Generation of Jet Fuel?
item.description: Scientists in Japan have turned discarded coconut oil into a sustainable aviation fuel that runs in a real jet engine, cuts pollution, and uses waste that would otherwise go to landfill.

item.title: How Did a Texas Barber Return $128,000 He Found at an ATM to Its Owner?
item.description: A man in Lewisville, Texas spotted a bag stuffed with over $128,000 in cash and checks sitting beside a Bank of America ATM. Without a second thought, he called the police and helped make sure every single dollar got back to its rightful owner.

item.title: How Did an Ancient Eclipse Show Earth Spun Faster 2,700 Years Ago?
item.description: A total solar eclipse witnessed by ancient Chinese astronomers in 709 BCE let researchers pin down how much faster Earth spun back then — and revealed that our star was waking up from a long quiet spell.

item.title: How Did Scientists Make Electric Car Batteries Smaller and Longer-Lasting?
item.description: South Korean researchers have borrowed super-precise computer-chip manufacturing to fix a major flaw in next-generation electric car batteries, potentially leading to smaller, lighter battery packs that let EVs travel farther on a single charge.

item.title: How Did White Storks Come Back to England After 600 Years Away?
item.description: A trio of juvenile white storks has arrived at Willington Wetlands in Derbyshire, marking the hopeful beginning of their return to the English Midlands after vanishing more than six centuries ago.

item.title: How Did Five Tiny Cheetah Cubs Make the Camera Their Playground?
item.description: A litter of five cheetah cubs born at the Smithsonian's conservation campus is now starring in a live den cam — offering a rare, up-close look at one of the world's most vulnerable big cats and the teamwork helping them survive.

item.title: What Makes a Fire Salamander Glow Under Ultraviolet Light?
item.description: Fire salamanders are famous for their bright warning colors, but scientists just discovered they do something magical under ultraviolet light: their skin and toxic secretions glow green and cyan, like nature's own neon sign.

item.title: How Do T Cells Feel Their Surroundings to Help Us Stay Healthy?
item.description: Scientists at McGill University discovered that T cells can feel how stiff or soft the tissues around them are. This 'hidden sense of touch' helps them decide whether to become long-lasting guards that protect us from future infections.

item.title: How Did Bomb-Testing Fingerprints End Up in Our Honey, Teeth, and Antarctic Ice?
item.description: Decades after atmospheric nuclear tests stopped, invisible radioactive fingerprints from the 1950s and 1960s still turn up in surprising places — from honey jars to baby teeth to Antarctic ice cores. Here's how scientists track these traces across the globe.

item.title: How Did a Stranger Pay $420 for a Group's Lunch in South Korea?
item.description: When 27 disabled residents and their caregivers from a community center in Incheon sat down for a barbecue lunch, they never expected a stranger to silently cover the bill — $420 worth of premium beef and all — before walking out without a word.

item.title: How Did a Tiny Scottish Island Become One of Early Christianity's Greatest Centers?
item.description: A small island in Scotland's Inner Hebrides was long known only from old stories and place names — but a community-led dig has uncovered the buried remains of a 6th-century monastery that rivaled Iona itself.

item.title: How Does an Autistic Brain Learn to Recognize Faces?
item.description: A new study using EEG brain scans found that autistic children's brains process faces differently than neurotypical children — and those differences may begin much earlier than scientists thought.

item.title: How Did Scientists Discover New Animals in a Lab, Airport, Cemetery, and Parking Lot?
item.description: From a neuroscience lab tank to a parking lot patch of moss, scientists are finding new species where we least expect them — even in our own backyards.

item.title: How Did a Luxury Cruise Ship End Up Stranded in Cambodia After Soaring Fuel Costs?
item.description: The Villa Vie Odyssey was more than 750 days into a 3.5-year journey around the world when rising fuel costs forced it to suspend operations in Cambodia.

item.title: 10 Amazing Animals Discovered in Places You'd Least Expect
item.description: From laboratory tanks to airport runways, new animal species turn up where we live, work, and travel — sometimes right under our noses.

item.title: How did a stretch of Antarctic water get named after a BBC science reporter?
item.description: A channel of water between two Antarctic islands now carries the name of Jonathan Amos, a BBC science correspondent who reported on polar research for nearly four decades.

item.title: How did four astronauts travel 100 million miles and come home safely?
item.description: After spending 237 days living and working aboard the International Space Station, four international astronauts safely splashed down in their Crew Dragon capsule — closing a mission that traveled more than 100 million miles around Earth.

item.title: How Did Tanzania Find Its First New Natural Gas in Over a Decade?
How Did a Teacher's Daily Positivity Practice Spread Through an Elementary School?
item.description: A first-grade teacher in Kansas started a simple daily affirmation circle — now children across every grade at Rex Elementary are ending their school day feeling confident and kind.
